children: By Nora Knoepflmacher | Photography by Jack Johnstone for WSJ. Magazine

At 19, Pierpaolo Seguso created his first glasswork in the furnaces of his family's glassblowing factory: an elaborate vase he named "Isola." Feeling the heavy glass in his palms, "there was a sense of pride and purpose," says Seguso, whose family has been a leader in the craft of Murano glassmaking for over 630 years.

As Murano island's glass factories face exorbitant energy costs, a shrinking pool of skilled apprentices and competition from counterfeits, the Seguso brand remains one of the last practitioners of the art form. Pierpaolo, the company's CEO and creative director, runs the business alongside his siblings Gianluca, Maria Giulia and Gianandrea.

In the early 1600s, the Seguso name was added to the Venetian government's Libro d'Oro, or Golden Book, granting them nobility for their glassmaking. Today, the brand's pieces have been showcased at the Venice Biennale and adorned the Vatican and hundreds of museums, including the Museum of Modern Art and the Victoria & Albert Museum. Pierpaolo studied architecture and has expanded the brand's catalog from lighting and accessories to interiors, including furniture, mirrors and hardware.

A stake of the Seguso brand was sold outside the family in the late '70s. Gianluca led the charge to buy it back in 2008. "It was the opportunity to go back to the archives and study a chapter of family legacy," says Pierpaolo.

Here, Pierpaolo Seguso, 52, who lives between Venice and New York, discusses his children joining the business, the family values he plans on passing down and adapting the brand for a modern consumer.
Did you always know that you were going to go into the family business?

Our father had a good way of engaging us without forcing us. He kept us close to the business but let us be free to do whatever we wanted. I studied architecture because that was my passion. There was a moment when I wanted to be an architect.
What role has Murano island played in the business?

The story of Seguso is very tied to the story of Murano. Sometimes I joke that besides the color of [our] shirt and [our] haircut, nothing else has changed. We still do artistic glass. Murano had an incredible role in providing the new use of [glass]: tabletops, mirrors, windows, the lens of Galileo's telescope, all of that artistic and technological engineering arrived to humanity thanks to this little island on the Venetian Lagoon and a group of people that we are part of.
What values are you passing on to your children?

In the time we're living in, it's very hard to understand the value of sacrifice. Everything is quick. There has to be a level of sacrifice, and you have to be willing to embrace it and enjoy that, which is the hardest part.
Do your children want to join the business?

They're young [13 and 15]. Sometimes it's yes, sometimes it's no. They know it's going to be a part of their life. I always tell them it's not their responsibility to carry it on. Their responsibility is to do what they like, be happy and do it to the highest of their ability.

When I started working, the bride registry was a big part of the business. All the high-end luxury department stores were a whole category of clients. That has totally disappeared. What is valuable has changed. You need to make your offerings interesting. Even for something that [people] don't necessarily need, our job is to keep it valuable, new, exciting and unique.
What was your experience visiting the factory when you were young?

Before I started working, Murano to me, was one door: my grandfather's factory. When I started working, I started learning what an incredible place it is. I remember seeing people doing things that were like magic. We still work with the old supplier from the island, many small workshops, to maintain the economy of the island but also because these are values that you don't want to get lost-the handmade, the ability to transform something basic into something unique.
